title: Essential Redis Commands
subtitle: GET, SET, DEL, KEYS, SCAN, EXPIRE, and TTL
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Knowing the data types is not enough — you need to know the commands to manipulate them. Each Redis type has its own command set, and some cross-cutting commands like EXPIRE, TTL, DEL, and SCAN apply to all keys.
whyItExists.solution: Redis provides a focused command vocabulary. Universal commands handle key lifecycle (expiry, deletion, renaming, scanning). Type-specific commands handle the structure itself.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time you interact with Redis from an application or the CLI, you are using these commands. Mastering them is prerequisite to everything else.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid KEYS * in production — it blocks the server while scanning the full keyspace. Use SCAN instead.

explainModes.beginner: Commands are like verbs for Redis. SET puts something in, GET takes it out, DEL removes it, EXPIRE schedules its auto-removal, and TTL checks how much time is left.
explainModes.simple: Every Redis command is <COMMAND> key [options]. Universal commands work on any key type: DEL, EXISTS, EXPIRE, TTL, RENAME, TYPE. Each data type also has its own command prefix: H for hashes, L for lists, S for sets, Z for sorted sets.
explainModes.standard: Redis commands follow a naming convention: command prefix indicates the type (H=hash, L=list, S=set, Z=zset) and the verb indicates the operation (GET, SET, ADD, POP, RANGE). Cross-type commands like EXPIRE, TTL, DEL, EXISTS, and SCAN apply universally.
explainModes.technical: Redis commands execute atomically in the single-threaded event loop. Commands are pipelined over TCP in the RESP (Redis Serialization Protocol) format. Time complexity is documented per command — O(1) for GET/SET, O(log N) for sorted set insertions, O(N) for LRANGE. SCAN is O(1) per call, O(N) overall (cursor-based iteration).
explainModes.deepDive: RESP3 (Redis 6+) adds support for push types and richer type information over the wire. Pipelining batches multiple commands without waiting for individual responses, reducing round-trip overhead. MULTI/EXEC provides optimistic transactions — commands queue atomically but see no isolation from concurrent writers between MULTI and EXEC.

content.text: These commands work on any key regardless of type. They manage the key lifecycle: existence, deletion, renaming, type inspection, and expiry.

content.code:
# Check existence
EXISTS user:1       # 1 if exists, 0 if not
EXISTS user:1 user:2 user:3  # count of existing keys

# Delete
DEL user:1          # deletes one key
DEL user:1 user:2   # deletes multiple
UNLINK user:1       # async delete (non-blocking, prefer for large keys)

# Inspect
TYPE user:1         # string, list, set, zset, hash, stream
OBJECT ENCODING user:1  # internal encoding

# Rename
RENAME old:key new:key   # overwrites new:key if exists
RENAMENX old:key new:key # only if new:key does not exist

content.text: Every Redis key can have a Time-To-Live (TTL). Redis automatically deletes expired keys. This is the foundation of caching.

content.code:
# Set with inline expiry (most common)
SET session:abc "data" EX 3600    # expire in 3600 seconds
SET otp:user1 "123456" PX 300000  # expire in 300000 ms (5 min)

# Add expiry to an existing key
EXPIRE session:abc 7200   # 2 hours from now
PEXPIRE session:abc 86400000  # 24 hours in milliseconds

# Expire at a Unix timestamp
EXPIREAT promo:sale 1735689600  # exact Unix timestamp

# Check remaining TTL
TTL session:abc   # seconds remaining (-1 = no expiry, -2 = key gone)
PTTL session:abc  # milliseconds remaining

# Remove expiry (make key permanent)
PERSIST session:abc

content.definition: The number of seconds (or milliseconds with PTTL) until Redis automatically deletes a key. Returns -1 if no expiry is set, -2 if the key does not exist.

content.text: Never use KEYS * in production. It blocks the entire Redis server while scanning all keys — with millions of keys, this freezes your application for seconds.

content.code:
# SCAN iterates safely (cursor-based, non-blocking)
# Returns a cursor + a batch of keys
SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
# Returns: 1) "2748"   (next cursor)
#          2) ["user:1", "user:2", ...]

# Keep scanning until cursor returns 0 (full iteration)
SCAN 2748 MATCH user:* COUNT 100
# ... repeat with returned cursor ...
SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100  # cursor 0 = complete

# Type-specific scan
HSCAN myhash 0 MATCH field:* COUNT 50
SSCAN myset 0 MATCH prefix:*
ZSCAN myzset 0 MATCH a*

content.text: Every Redis command requires a network round-trip. Pipelining batches multiple commands into one network request, dramatically improving throughput for bulk operations.
Use UNLINK instead of DEL for large keys (big lists, hashes). UNLINK removes the key immediately from the keyspace but frees memory asynchronously in the background.

questions.question: What does TTL return when a key exists but has no expiry set?
questions.explanation: TTL returns -1 for keys that exist but have no expiry. It returns -2 if the key does not exist at all.

questions.question: Why should you use SCAN instead of KEYS * in production?
options: KEYS * blocks the server while scanning all keys; SCAN iterates without blocking
questions.explanation: Redis is single-threaded. KEYS * scans all keys in one shot, blocking all other commands. SCAN uses a cursor and returns results in small batches.

questions.question: What is the difference between DEL and UNLINK?
options: DEL is for strings, UNLINK is for lists
DEL removes keys synchronously; UNLINK removes from keyspace immediately but frees memory asynchronously
UNLINK only works on expired keys
DEL returns the value, UNLINK does not
questions.explanation: UNLINK is a non-blocking version of DEL. The key disappears immediately from the keyspace but actual memory deallocation happens in a background thread, so it doesn't block the event loop.

faq.q: How do I rename a key?
faq.a: RENAME oldkey newkey. If newkey already exists it is overwritten. Use RENAMENX to only rename if newkey does not exist.

faq.q: How do I copy a key?
faq.a: COPY source destination [DB db] [REPLACE]. Available since Redis 6.2.

faq.q: Can I set expiry on a hash field?
faq.a: Not in standard Redis. TTL applies to the whole key. Redis 7.4+ added HEXPIRE for field-level expiry, but it is not yet widely available on managed services.

examples: Storing a password-reset token with a 15-minute expiry using SET token:xyz EX 900
Scanning all user keys nightly for cleanup using SCAN with MATCH user:* without blocking
